newsitem.title: ITALY: Ex-Nazi Priebke given house arrest in Italy.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Nazi Priebke given house arrest in Italy.

text.p: A military court ruled on Tuesday that former SS officer Erich Priebke could be freed from jail and held under house arrest pending a re-trial for Italy's worst World War Two atrocity.

Military prosecutor Antonino Intelisano, who has led the case against Priebke, said the judges decided in closed-door session to grant a defence request to release him from prison because of worsening mental health.
"Obviously he is very satisfied, especially for his wife's sake," defence attorney Giosue Naso told Reuters. "This makes it much more possible for him to hug his wife again soon."

Priebke, 83, has been detained since his extradition in November 1995 from Argentina where he had lived openly since 1948. Naso said he was expected to be released from Rome's Forte Boccea military prison on Wednesday or Thursday.

Judicial sources said Priebke was likely to be housed in a Roman Catholic convent or monastery until the re-trial, which Naso said would begin in Rome on April 14 together with that of another ex-Nazi, former SS captain Karl Hass.
Both men are charged with complicity in the multiple murder of 335 men and boys in the Ardeatine Caves in March 1944. Seventy-five of the victims were Jews.
Both have admitted shooting victims but say they would have been killed themselves if they failed to obey orders. Hass, 84, is already being held under house arrest in Rome.
Giulia Spizzichino, who lost seven relatives in the massacre, said the decision to let Priebke out of jail was unfair. "Everywhere he goes, he always falls on his feet," she said.
The Simon Wiesenthal Center in Los Angeles, which tracks down former Nazis, described the court ruling as "outrageous".
"This is not your average Nazi war criminal," Rabbi Abraham Cooper said by telephone from Los Angeles. "He deserves to stay in jail every single day for the rest of his life. Period."
Defence lawyers said they presented medical reports to the court pointing to a loss of Priebke's mental powers because of isolation and advancing age.
A military court tried Priebke last year for the massacre and ruled that he was guilty but should be allowed to go free because of extenuating circumstances which triggered a statute of limitations.
The verdict caused outrage and led to Priebke's re-arrest after relatives of the victims laid siege to the courthouse. The verdict was quashed in October on appeal.
